edges.description: Y. pestis uses its type III secretion system to subvert early mammalian host defenses after inoculation.
edges.target: Type III Secretion-Mediated Innate Immune Evasion

edges.description: In the mammalian host, the Pla outer-membrane protease can activate fibrinolysis and remodel the host hemostatic environment in ways that support dissemination.
Yop-mediated immune evasion permits extracellular Y. pestis survival and replication, supporting dissemination to the draining lymph node.
edges.source: Type III Secretion-Mediated Innate Immune Evasion

edges.description: Fibrinolysis and reduced fibrin deposition plausibly help bacteria leave the inoculation site and reach the lymphatic drainage basin.
Regional lymph-node replication clinically produces the lymphadenopathy named the bubo.
Lymph-node Y. pestis replication and the associated inflammatory response can contribute to systemic febrile symptoms.
Lymph-node Y. pestis replication and the associated inflammatory response can contribute to chills as a systemic acute-infection symptom.
Y. pestis can leave the lymphatic focus and spread into the bloodstream.
Bloodstream spread of Y. pestis can produce septicemic plague and clinical sepsis.
Severe bloodstream plague can progress to septic coagulopathy.
Coagulopathy and shock in disseminated plague can cause acral ischemic necrosis.

nodes.description: Regional lymphadenopathy caused by the lymph-node infection that defines bubonic plague.
Bacteria reach regional lymph nodes and replicate there; this lymphatic focus is the anatomic process that produces the bubo of bubonic plague.

evidence.reference_title: Yersinia pestis and plague: an updated view on evolution, virulence determinants, immune subversion, vaccination, and diagnostics.
evidence.snippet: unrestricted bacterial replication in lymph nodes (bubonic plague) and in lungs (pneumonic plague)

nodes.description: Infected fleas transmit Y. pestis from rodent reservoirs and inoculate the bacterium into skin, initiating the usual route to bubonic plague through local survival, hemostatic remodeling, and dissemination to a draining lymph node.

evidence.reference_title: Yersinia pestis and plague: an updated view on evolution, virulence determinants, immune subversion, vaccination, and diagnostics.
evidence.snippet: Plague is a vector-borne disease caused by Yersinia pestis. Transmitted by fleas from rodent reservoirs

nodes.description: Y. pestis can disseminate from the lymphatic focus into the bloodstream, producing systemic plague and sepsis.

The Pla omptin protease activates human plasminogen and urokinase while inactivating the host fibrinolysis inhibitors alpha-2-antiplasmin and plasminogen activator inhibitor 1, enhancing local fibrinolysis that is thought to promote Y. pestis survival and spread from the dermal inoculation site.

evidence.reference_title: Fibrinolytic and coagulative activities of Yersinia pestis.
evidence.snippet: Pla activates human plasminogen to the serine protease plasmin and activates the physiological plasminogen activator urokinase.

nodes.description: The Y. pestis type III secretion system injects Yop effector proteins into mammalian host cells and suppresses phagocyte defenses, permitting bacterial survival and expansion.
nodes.id: Type III Secretion-Mediated Innate Immune Evasion

evidence.reference_title: The Yersinia pestis type III secretion system: expression, assembly and role in the evasion of host defenses.
evidence.snippet: Yersinia pestis, the etiologic agent of plague, utilizes a type III secretion system (T3SS) to subvert the defenses of its mammalian hosts.
